subject: Procrustes ANOVA for two crossed factors with one being random

messages.author: 6180ccabbdf86586
messages.subject: Procrustes ANOVA for two crossed factors with one being random
parts:
In geomorph vignette "Addition by subtraction", there is the following code:
fit.common <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + treatment/family, data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE)
Since family is a random effect nested within the fixed effect treatment, main effect of treatment is tested with updated F-value denominator MS_Treatment:Family. 

I am wondering if every family received each level of treatment, i.e., treatment and family are crossed rather than nested, but family is still a random effect, how should I rewirte fit.common. 
Is fit.common2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + treatment*family, data = gdf) correct? How should I update denominator for all terms?

If I have only one fixed effect of treatment and want to consider all specimens as random realization of all possible samples of the same size, how should I test the effect of treatment? fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ treatment) is what is normally done but this does not seem to reflect the random nature of the specimens.

Thanks.


Kieran

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA for two crossed factors with one being random
parts:
Hi Kieran,

You are correct that if every family received every level of treatment, you can set up your linear model either with crossing or nesting.  Here is how to do it either way:

 fit.common2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + family * treatment, data = gdf) # crossing

 fit.common2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + family + treatment/family, data = gdf) # nesting

Using type II or type III SS will produce the same SS with either model above; using type I SS will alter the SS, based on term order.  (The columns of the design matrix are the same in both cases but not in the same order.)

You could perform ANOVA as

anova(fit.common2)

but the test for treatment might not be appropriate, as it assumes all terms are fixed.  You can do something, like

anova(fit.common2, error = c(“Residuals”, “Residuals”, “family:treatment”, “Residuals”)

to adjust the F values of treatment to be calculated with respect to random effects, rather than residuals.  This is explained in the vignette but note that it was based on the formula you originally used.  The point is that the solution is not in how you set up the formula but how you adjust the F values in ANOVA.

Hope that helps.

Mike

parts:
Thank you Mike, that is pretty clear. I could understand the formula in the vignettes as well as your explanations. I have got a related question on the formula for ANOVA in bilat.symmetry function.

In cases of no replication, bilat.symmetry uses form.shape <- Y ~ ind + side as the formula for procD.lm, which I could understand. But when there is replication, the formula used was form.shape <- Y ~ ind + side + ind/side. According to model output, ind/side reflects FA. But why using ind/side rather than ind:side? ind/side seems to suggest taking side as a random effect nested in the fixed effect of ind. This is somewhat counterintuitive. Side should be fixed and ind should be random, which mean side/ind is more appropriate?

Kieran

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA for two crossed factors with one being random
parts:
Kieran,

Sorry, I missed your follow up question.  There really is no difference in the two styles.  In fact, R has a particular way of expanding equations.

~ a * b

is expanded to 

~ a + b + a:b

and

~ a/b

is expanded to 

~ a + a:b

If you expand the equation on your own, using ~ a + b + a/b, this is what R does:

> terms(~ a + b + a/b)
~a + b + a/b
attr(,"variables")
list(a, b)
attr(,"factors")
  a b a:b
a 1 0   1
b 0 1   1
attr(,"term.labels")
[1] "a"   "b"   "a:b"
attr(,"order")
[1] 1 1 2
attr(,"intercept")
[1] 1
attr(,"response")
[1] 0
attr(,".Environment")
<environment: R_GlobalEnv>

Meaning, that R changes a/b to a:b.  They are the same.  Your concern with notation has no implication for the results.  But, concerning your notation, you are right that we should probably use ind:side or side:ind (again the same), since this is how R changes it.

Regarding nesting more generally, I think assigning “fixed” or “random” terms to a design like this can be misleading (I think both are random effects).  I found the following that might help explain the concept (using lme4):

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/228800/crossed-vs-nested-random-effects-how-do-they-differ-and-how-are-they-specified

There is a good demonstration for the difference between nested and crossed designs, with the caveat, "Nesting is a property of the data, or rather the experimental design, not the model.”  In the example, there is a design where data are collected from classes nested within schools.  Even if class 1 = math and class 2 = literature, taught at each school, class is still nested within school rather than school nested within class, even though doing either could result in the same model, depending on other terms in the model.  Likewise, left sides or right sides are inherent attributes of individuals.  I try to think of it in a hierarchal context rather than forcing a “fixed” label on some part of it.  Thus, ind/side demonstrates the hierarchy.  

Nevertheless, I would agree that ind:side or side:ind is more precise to inform the model rather than the design and something we should consider.  

Thanks for provoking this!

Mike
